stories.title: Salesforce Acquires Cresta for ~$2.7B to Add Voice AI to Agentforce
stories.body: On November 2, 2026, Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Cresta, reportedly valued at $2.7 billion, folding Cresta's voice agents and real-time rep-guidance platform into Service Cloud and Agentforce. Cresta's enterprise customers include Marriott, Comcast, and Alaska Airlines; closing is expected in Salesforce's Q1 fiscal 2028. Cresta will continue to support the contact-center and telephony platforms its existing customers already use, though analysts note the deal puts Salesforce in direct competition with contact-center partners and removes one of the larger independent voice-AI specialists from the market.
stories.why: Cresta is a named competitor in enterprise CX AI — its absorption into Salesforce's Agentforce stack changes the vendor shortlist overnight, and retail accounts running non-Salesforce CRM now face an uncertain roadmap. A seller can use this to open the 'platform lock-in vs. best-of-breed' conversation and position a neutral, data-layer-first approach that works regardless of which CRM the retailer runs.

stories.title: Sierra Closes $1.75B Series F at $30B Valuation as ARR Tops $400M
stories.body: Sierra Technologies raised $1.75 billion led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners on November 23, 2026, nearly doubling its $15.8 billion May valuation to $30 billion — its third raise in 14 months. Annual recurring revenue has passed $400 million, up from $100 million in November 2025, and Sierra charges only when its agents deliver outcomes. The same week saw Decagon ($4.5B valuation, January 2026) and Parloa ($3B valuation, January 2026) also active, confirming that the customer-service agent category is consolidating around a small set of well-capitalised pure-plays.
stories.why: Sierra is the benchmark competitor in outcome-based enterprise AI agents; its pricing model ('pay only when agents deliver') is increasingly the expectation buyers bring to every agent-vendor conversation. A Graas seller must be ready to articulate what differentiates a retail-domain context layer from Sierra's general-purpose agent infrastructure — Sierra's agents still depend on whatever data foundation the retailer has built.

stories.title: Gartner 2026 CIO Agenda for Retail: 48% Plan Agentic AI Deployment, Only 39% Have the Data Foundation to Support It
stories.body: Gartner's 2026 CIO Agenda for Retail finds that 48% of retail respondents plan to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, yet only 39% of retailers have both a data strategy and an operating model to support it — leaving 61% structurally unready. Gartner separately predicts that 40% of agentic AI projects enterprise-wide will be canceled by 2027 due to governance failures and unclear ROI, and quotes the barrier plainly: 'Without accurate and timely data, particularly from the store, AI initiatives stall.' Retail CIOs nonetheless plan to raise AI spending by 36% and generative AI spending by 38% in 2026.
stories.why: This is the single most quotable analyst finding for a retail-AI sales call: the ambition-to-readiness gap (48% want agents, only 39% have the data layer) is the exact problem a context-layer or data-foundation sale solves. The 40% cancellation forecast gives urgency — buyers need to get their data infrastructure right before they scale agents, not after.

stories.title: McKinsey State of AI 2026: Only 37% of Companies See EBIT Impact Despite 80% Reporting Productivity Gains
stories.body: McKinsey's 2026 State of AI report finds that 40% of large enterprises are now scaling AI agents in at least one function, up from 27% a year ago, but only 37% of respondents report any impact on company EBIT — roughly the same share as in 2025. The report identifies AI high performers (just 6% of respondents) as 3.3x more likely to plan fundamental transformation, and nearly three-quarters of those high performers have redesigned workflows around AI versus one-quarter of other companies. Separately, 32% of organizations say they have decided against buying at least one software product because they believe they can build it in-house using agentic coding tools.
stories.why: The productivity-to-profit gap ('80% say productive, only 37% see EBIT impact') is a powerful conversation-opener for why agents without a governed data foundation produce noise, not margin. The build-vs-buy finding — 32% choosing internal builds — is a direct challenge for every enterprise AI vendor, including Graas: sellers must be prepared to show why a purpose-built retail context layer beats a homegrown LLM wrapper.

stories.title: Gartner Names Context Graphs the Essential Backbone for Agentic AI; Atlan Publishes Implementation Guide
stories.body: In a November 17, 2026 implementation guide, Atlan documents that Gartner now formally recognises context graphs as the essential backbone for agentic AI and names Atlan among the exemplar vendors defining the category. The guide argues that 95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to deliver measurable P&L impact, and that the fix is not a better model but a governed Enterprise Data Graph — a metadata lakehouse plus graph engine — exposed to agents via MCP servers, semantic search, or RAG pipelines. Siemens/RapidMiner published a parallel architecture piece positioning an enterprise-scale knowledge graph (not a point-solution graph database) as the universal context layer, noting that agents need context spanning the entire enterprise, not a single department.
stories.why: Gartner's formal category recognition of 'context graphs' gives a Graas seller third-party validation for the exact architecture argument — that agents fail without a shared, governed knowledge layer, not a model problem. The MCP-exposure pattern described here is exactly how a retail context layer (SKU, inventory, identity) must be surfaced to any agent vendor, including Sierra or Agentforce, making this a foundation story that complements, not competes with, the agent vendors above.
